title: How the Electoral College Actually Works

scenes.label: Hook
scenes.narration: In five American elections, the winner of the popular vote lost the presidency.

scenes.label: Basics
scenes.narration: Each state gets electoral votes equal to its senators plus its representatives.

scenes.label: The magic number
scenes.narration: Five hundred thirty eight votes total. You need two hundred seventy to win.

scenes.label: Winner take all
scenes.narration: In most states, whoever wins the popular vote takes all of that state's electors.

scenes.label: Swing states
scenes.narration: So candidates ignore safe states and campaign almost only in swing states.

scenes.label: Outro
scenes.narration: That is the electoral college, in sixty seconds.

scenes.label: Introduction
scenes.narration: Welcome to Political Animation. Today: the electoral college — the most misunderstood part of American presidential elections.

scenes.label: Origins in 1787
scenes.narration: The founders created the electoral college at the Constitutional Convention as a compromise between electing the president by Congress or by popular vote.

scenes.label: How votes are allocated
scenes.narration: Each state gets electors equal to its congressional delegation: two senators, plus however many representatives it has. Washington D.C. gets three.

scenes.label: Winner-take-all
scenes.narration: Forty-eight states and D.C. use winner-take-all: the statewide popular vote winner takes every elector. Maine and Nebraska split theirs by congressional district.

scenes.label: When the popular vote lost
scenes.narration: It has happened five times: 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016. In 2000, George W. Bush won the presidency with fewer votes than Al Gore.

scenes.label: The swing state map
scenes.narration: Because most states are safe, campaigns focus almost entirely on a handful of swing states — Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona, Georgia, Nevada.

scenes.label: Faithless electors
scenes.narration: Electors are pledged to a candidate, but occasionally one votes faithlessly. In 2020 the Supreme Court ruled states can punish or replace them.

scenes.label: Reform ideas
scenes.narration: Reform proposals include the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, or abolishing the electoral college entirely by constitutional amendment.

scenes.label: Outro
scenes.narration: That is the electoral college. Subscribe for more explainers on US politics.
